lines.name: The Woman Who Sold Herself Twice

scenes.prose:
NOBODY'S WITNESS

Blackwood — population four thousand, and falling

Act One — The Woman Who Sold Herself Twice

scenes.title: Part 1 — The Woman Who Sold Herself Twice
scenes.prose: Rain on glass, a ceiling fan ticking in slow lazy circles, a diner hum underneath. Eleven forty-seven. Same booth most nights, phone turned face-down.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, from somewhere further on
dialogueBeats.text: Nobody took what I lost. I handed it over. In order. So when I tell you I didn't see it coming — I saw it. That's the only thing I need you to believe.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — settling into the scene, still spare
dialogueBeats.text: Eleven forty-seven. Blackwood Diner. Same booth most nights, phone turned face-down because I already know who's not calling.

Blackwood. Mill closed in '09, then everything that fed it. Four thousand people left, a clinic with a waiting list, and Solomon Reyes, who employs more of this town than the county does. Nobody here's bad. They're hungry. Different thing.
She didn't scan the room. Walked straight to my booth. Like she'd already had this conversation in her head a few times before her body caught up.
They told me you're the only one in this town who doesn't work for Solomon Reyes.
Who's they.
Just people, you know how they talk. and they all said it the same way, like it was the only thing about you worth Knowing........ Vera Voss
Mrs. Voss. That make this personal or professional?
I looked up. Not beautiful, exactly — held together with both hands, hoping nobody noticed the effort.
What can I do for you.

dialogueBeats.expression: straightforward, no games, a small crack in the composure
dialogueBeats.text: My husband's missing. Three weeks now. Cops filed it, did nothing, told me he probably just left. I don't believe that. And I need somebody better than the cops to find out if I'm wrong.
Missing people usually want to stay missing. You sure you want him found?
I want to know where he is. What I feel about that once I know is my own business.
First real answer all night. And I remember deciding, right there, that I was going to believe her. Not that I did. That I was going to.
Name?
David Voss.

choices.text: Say nothing. Keep working the file.

scenes.title: Part 1 — The Woman Who Sold Herself Twice

dialogueBeats.text: I knew the name. Blackwood's four thousand people and half of them owe Solomon Reyes something — David Voss ran his money, everybody knew that the way you know which houses have somebody in them. So a man who works for Solomon disappears, and his wife comes to the one person in town who isn't owned by Solomon. That's not a coincidence. That's a shape.
I looked at the shape for about as long as it takes to read this sentence, and then I put it somewhere I wouldn't have to look at it again, and I asked her what he was wearing when she saw him last.
Your husband do business with Solomon Reyes?
Yes.

dialogueBeats.expression: a little surprised she just said it
dialogueBeats.text: Most people dance around that question.
I'm not most people. I don't have time to dance, Mr. Morrow. I have three weeks of nothing and a folder full of everything I could find. You want to help me or not?
I liked her for that.
One thing first. Your three people. Did any of them tell you why I don't work for him, or did they just leave it at the fact?
They said you were a detective for sixteen years and then you weren't, and that Solomon had something to do with which one it was. Nobody said more than that.
There was a file. Solomon's name in it. I was asked to lose it. Didn't. Asked again by somebody higher up. Didn't again.
And?
Nobody charged me with anything. Isn't how it works here. They just made me somebody nothing gets assigned to. Eleven months at that desk. Then I quit and called it a decision.
And the file?
Lost. Just not by me. That's the part I got to keep.

That's the whole story. People in Blackwood think it's tragic. It isn't. Tragic would've been fast. What actually happened is I said no to a thing one time, correctly, and then nothing else happened to me for ten years.

dialogueBeats.expression: leaning back, gentler this time, not testing her so much as actually asking
dialogueBeats.text: You're awfully calm for a woman whose husband might be hiding from a guy like Reyes.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, and for a second, something real underneath the control
dialogueBeats.text: I've had three weeks to get calm about it. Don't mistake it for not caring. I care. I just don't have anybody left to fall apart in front of.
Truth and performance, same room, taking turns. I picked. I want that on the record.

scenes.title: Part 1 — The Woman Who Sold Herself Twice
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 1 — The Woman Who Sold Herself Twice
scenes.prose: Rain against the window. The folder, a hand's width from his.

dialogueBeats.text: Alright. Two hundred a day plus expenses. I find him, I tell you where he is. What you do after that's yours to carry.

dialogueBeats.expression: standing, sliding the folder the rest of the way to him
dialogueBeats.text: Thank you. I mean that.
You always this easy to negotiate with?

dialogueBeats.expression: putting her coat back into place, something unreadable and a little sad in her face
dialogueBeats.text: No. You just haven't asked for anything worth fighting over yet.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, her footsteps retreating, the bell chiming
dialogueBeats.text: No napkin, no line. A folder, a name I didn't like, and a woman too honest to be lying about all of it.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, papers shifting, a long exhale
dialogueBeats.text: Smart move was letting it go. I'm not smart about that.
Lonely, dressed up as a work ethic. I turned the page.

choices.text: The Blue Cue. First name on the list.

scenes.title: Part 1 (alt) — The Description
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 1 (alt) — The Description
scenes.prose: Rain. The fan. Jack going still for half a second.

dialogueBeats.text: I knew the name. Blackwood's four thousand people and half of them owe Solomon Reyes something — David Voss ran his money, everybody knew that the way you know which houses have somebody in them.
You'll have a photo in there.
I'll have a photo. I want it from you.
Why.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat before the last sentence
dialogueBeats.text: Because a photo tells me what a man looked like on the day somebody took it. You've been married eleven years.
She picks up the coffee she hasn't touched all night, and doesn't drink it.
He was about six foot. Six one.
Jack's pen stopping.

dialogueBeats.expression: continuing, not noticing — or noticing perfectly
dialogueBeats.text: He had a scar through the left eyebrow — bike, when he was nine. His hands were bigger than they should have been for his size. People used to say that.
Used to.
People say that.
Rain. The fan. Neither of them moving.
There it is. Three days into this job I'd have caught that in my sleep. It took me four seconds and I let it go past.
Is that useful?
It's a start.
Her standing. The booth releasing. The folder sliding across.
Two hundred a day, you said.
Plus expenses.

dialogueBeats.expression: at the edge of the booth, and this is the only time in the film she sounds uncertain — a beat after 'don't like'
dialogueBeats.text: Mr. Morrow. If you find something you don't like — I'd rather hear it from you than from anybody else. That's all I'm asking for on top.
That's not an unusual thing to ask.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat before the last sentence
dialogueBeats.text: No. It's what everybody asks. Hardly anybody means it.
The bell. The door. Rain swelling, then muffled.
She'd talked about him in the past tense and then corrected it, and asked me to bring bad news to her personally, and I let her walk out into the rain.
Rain. The fan. Jack not opening the folder.

I didn't open the folder that night. I've thought about why. Best I can manage is: the folder was hers, and I'd just watched her be careless in front of me for four seconds, and I wanted to see the careless one again before I read the careful one.
Coins on the table. A chair. Footsteps.
So I followed her home.

scenes.title: Part 1 (alt) — The One Who Said No
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 1 (alt) — The One Who Said No
scenes.prose: The folder on the table between them. Neither hand on it.

dialogueBeats.text: No?
Can I ask you something first. Have you been to the depot?
Day two. And the clinic, and both bars he used, and his sister in Fairview who hasn't spoken to him since March. I've done all of it, Mr. Morrow. I'm not an idiot.
No. You're not. That's the problem.
The fan. Rain on the window.

Three weeks of looking, and this is what it produced. Bank statements in order. Four names, addresses attached. A timeline. Mrs. Voss, I've seen a hundred of these and they're all a mess, because that's what three weeks of a frightened person looks like. It's receipts and a shoebox and things written on the back of other things.
dialogueBeats.expression: flat, tapping the folder without opening it — a beat after timeline

dialogueBeats.text: And?
This isn't a search. It's a finished argument. Somebody made this to be read by somebody, and I'd want to know who it's addressed to before I'm the one reading it.
A long pause. The fan.
And that's a reason to say no.

That, and I know who your husband collects for. I've been on the wrong side of Solomon Reyes once already. It cost me eleven months and it very nearly cost me the office. I'm not a brave man, Mrs. Voss. I'm just an expensive one.
dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after collects for, a beat after office

dialogueBeats.text: The fan. Rain on the window.
I could tell you what's in it. Right now. All of it.
I know. That's the other reason. You'd tell me, and it'd be good, and I'd take the job. Sixteen years, Mrs. Voss — the trick isn't spotting it. The trick's not listening to the next part.
A long silence.
That's fair.
I'm sorry.
Don't be. You're the first person in this town who's been straight with me in about nine years. It's just poor timing.
dialogueBeats.expression: standing, taking the folder back — a beat after Don't be

dialogueBeats.text: Her footsteps. The bell. The door. Rain swelling — then muffled.
And that was it. The first no I'd said to a paying client in two years, and I'd meant every word of it.

scenes.note: Refusal route. Delay, not a fork. Jack never follows her. Merges at the Blue Cue.

scenes.title: Part 1 (alt) — She Didn't Start the Car
scenes.prose: The fan. Rain. Jack still in the booth.

dialogueBeats.text: I didn't follow her. I stayed where I was. But I watched her the whole way across that lot, and I'd like to tell you that was instinct. It wasn't. I'd just turned her down and I wasn't ready for the last of her to be a door closing.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after I stayed where I was

dialogueBeats.text: She got in her car and she didn't start it.
Rain on the glass. The fan.
A woman who's been turned down drives off annoyed. Two minutes, maybe. She sat there eleven.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after maybe

dialogueBeats.text: A long hold. Nothing happens.
Eleven minutes is not being upset. Eleven minutes is a person who hasn't got a next place to go and is working out how to pretend she has.
Finally — an engine starting. Headlights sweeping the diner window. Gone.

I sat there another twenty minutes after she'd gone. Turned the coffee round on the table a few times. Told myself I'd done the right thing, which is a sentence you only need to say if you're not sure.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after gone

action.text: Interior light off. Engine off. She's in it. A woman with somewhere to be would already be gone.

dialogueBeats.text: I didn't go to the house. I went home and I sat with the no until morning made it look cheaper than it was.

scenes.title: Part 1 (alt) — The Door
scenes.prose: Morning. Rain finished. Wet street, traffic somewhere distant. Footsteps on stairs.

dialogueBeats.text: It was on the door when I got in the next morning. Taped at eye level, which is a decision somebody makes.
Second notice. Fourteen days. Sal Hirsch doesn't send a third one — he sends two men and a van, and he's never once been unreasonable about it, which is the part that stings.
Tape peeling. Paper folding. A door unlocking.
I sat down at a desk I'd got fourteen days left on and I did the only sum available. Two hundred a day. Fourteen days. It isn't even close. It's not a decision, it's a receipt.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after available

dialogueBeats.text: A chair. A drawer. Rain starting again on the blind.

Here's what I'd like to be able to tell you: that I turned her down for good reasons and picked her up again for bad ones, and that the notice on the door was what changed it. The notice made it easy. That's different from making it happen.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet — a beat after changed it

action.text: SECOND NOTICE. Fourteen days. Sal doesn't send a third. He sends two men and a van.

dialogueBeats.text: One Voss in the book and it's in her name, not his. I noticed that and I didn't do anything with it, which is going to be a pattern.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after not his

dialogueBeats.text: A phone book. Pages. A receiver lifted. Numbers dialled.
Ringing. Four times.
Yes.
It's Morrow.
A pause on the line.
Alright.
I was wrong last night.
A pause on the line. She doesn't ask about what.
Alright.
You're not going to ask me why.
dialogueBeats.expression: waiting a beat for a question that doesn't come

dialogueBeats.text: No. You had a reason last night and now you've got a different one. They're both yours.
dialogueBeats.expression: filtered, phone — flat — a beat after No

dialogueBeats.text: The fan on her end. Or a radio. Something domestic.
Two hundred a day plus expenses. I find him, I tell you where he is. What you do after that's yours to carry.
Yes.
The folder.
It's at the diner. Behind the counter. I left it with the girl on the morning shift.
A beat.
The diner.
You're there at a quarter to twelve most nights, Mr. Morrow. It's a small town. You said so yourself.
dialogueBeats.expression: filtered, phone — flat — a beat after Morrow

dialogueBeats.text: The line going dead. Rain on the blind.
She hadn't posted it, hadn't dropped it at the office, hadn't kept hold of it. She'd left it in the one building in this town where she knew I'd be sitting anyway, whether I rang her or not.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after hold of it

dialogueBeats.text: Rain.
I've had people find out where I drink. Nobody's ever used it to be polite before.

dialogueBeats.text: The diner at two in the afternoon is a different building. Sun through the window, kids in a booth, somebody's radio on behind the counter. The waitress handed it over without looking up and said a lady left it, and went back to what she was doing.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after counter

dialogueBeats.text: Pages. A door. The street.
No napkin, no big line. A folder from behind a counter, a name I didn't like, and a woman who heard the word no and left it out for me anyway.
A car door. An engine.
Smart move was letting it go. I'd already made the smart move once and it bought me a notice on the door and the longest night of a quiet year. Lonely, dressed up as a work ethic.
dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet — a beat after year

action.text: Behind the counter, with the morning girl. Squared to the edge like she'd practiced leaving it somewhere she'd walk past anyway.

scenes.title: Part 2 — The Wrong Kind of Regulars
scenes.prose: A pool hall. Balls clacking, a jukebox playing something old and warped, ice clinking in a glass somewhere. A single hanging lamp over the table, everything else in shadow. Wasn't blue. Cue wasn't even straight.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — settling into narration, dry but easy
dialogueBeats.text: Folder had a list of David Voss's known associates. Polite way of saying "people who'll lie to a detective if the price is right." First name led me to a place called The Blue Cue. Wasn't blue. Cue wasn't even straight.
Two guys at the bar. Didn't need a badge or a gun to know what they did for a living. One built like a filing cabinet. Other one built like the guy who tells the filing cabinet where to stand.
I'm telling you, man, self-checkout is a scam. They didn't build those machines to save you time. They built 'em so you do the cashier's job for free and thank 'em on the way out.
Nobody's thanking a machine, Desh.
You ever say sorry to one? "Unexpected item in the bagging area," and you go, "oh — my bad." That's not shopping, man, that's conditioning.
It's a scale. It weighs your bag.
And who told you that's all it does — the machine? You trust the machine's word for it now?
Two men who hurt people for a living, arguing about grocery stores.
Help you with something.
Looking for a guy. David Voss. You know him?
Never heard of him.
Heard the name once.
We said never heard of him, man. That's the line today.
Forgot which line we were on.
Never heard of him.
Nobody lies that bad on accident. That's a skill.
Here's my problem. Somebody's paying me good money to find a guy nobody's ever heard of. Feels like a waste of everybody's time.

dialogueBeats.expression: calm, but with an edge now — the glass coming down deliberate and heavy
dialogueBeats.text: You know what I think, Mr. —
Morrow.
— Mr. Morrow. I think you finish whatever the hell you're not drinking, and you walk out that door. That's the version of tonight where you're still breathing tomorrow.

action.text: Something old and warped. It plays a recording, Desh. That's all it is.
Moe and Desh at the bar, backs to the door, silhouetted against a dead neon beer sign. Smoke hanging still in the light.

scenes.title: Part 2 — The Wrong Kind of Regulars
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 2 — The Wrong Kind of Regulars
scenes.prose: The lamp over the table. The jukebox. Rain outside.

dialogueBeats.text: And I really do have more to say about the self-checkout thing, if you wanna stick around for that instead.
I believed him. That was somehow the scarier offer.
Appreciate the hospitality. Tell your boss I said hi. Guessing he already knows I stopped by.
He knew before you sat down.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quieter, more serious, out in the rain
dialogueBeats.text: What actually stuck with me wasn't the threat. It was that nobody in that bar flinched when I said David Voss's name was tied to my client. Nobody asked who my client was. Which meant somebody already told them. And the only person who knew I was working this case was the woman who hired me.
So here it is, and then I won't do this again.

I knew who she was before she sat down. Knew whose wife she was. Knew a man doesn't run from Solomon Reyes and leave a folder that tidy behind him, and I knew a woman who wanted her husband found in a town this size asks at the depot and the clinic and she's got him by Tuesday. I knew all of that in the first four minutes. I have known things for a living for sixteen years and I have never once been wrong this fast.

And I took the folder anyway. Because the alternative was saying it out loud, and if I said it out loud she'd stand up, and then I'd be a man sitting alone in a diner at eleven forty-seven the same as I was the night before. Ten years of that. You'd have taken the folder too.
That's the last honest thing I'm going to say for a while. Everything after this, I was lying to myself on purpose, and I'd rather you watched me do it than had me explain it.

scenes.title: Part 2 (alt) — The Name
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 2 (alt) — The Name
scenes.prose: The jukebox. Balls clacking somewhere. Nothing else changes at all.

dialogueBeats.text: I said it to watch his face. That's the whole reason. Sixteen years and I have never once given a client up, and I did it in a pool hall to see whether a man would blink.
Moe setting his glass down. Unhurried.
Alright.
That mean anything to you?
Means you've got a client.
Means you've got a client and now we've got a Tuesday.
Jack shifting. The jukebox track ending, clicking over.
What's that supposed to mean.
Nothing. Desh talks.
A long silence. Rain outside.

Nothing happened in his face. I want to be exact about this, because I spent a long time afterward trying to remember a flicker. There wasn't one. He heard the name and it went somewhere and his face stayed where it was, and I stood there thinking I'd got nothing.
Jack standing. A stool scraping back.
Mr. Morrow.
Yeah.
You shouldn't have done that.
Rain. The door. The bell.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'Nineteen hours'
dialogueBeats.text: Nineteen hours. That's how long she had, and I gave it away in a pool hall, for free, to see a man blink.

scenes.title: Part 3 — A Trail Too Clean to Trust
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 3 — A Trail Too Clean to Trust
scenes.prose: A cramped office at night. One lamp, a wide pool of yellow light, everything past its edge black. Bank statements fanned out like a hand of cards. His face lit from below, tired.

dialogueBeats.text: Spent the next two nights doing the part of this job nobody puts in the movies. Just me, a desk lamp, and a folder full of somebody else's life, reading it line by line like I was checking it for typos, or maybe just looking for a reason not to believe what I was starting to believe.

Bank statements first. David Voss pulled six grand out four days before he vanished. Fine — people do that when they're running. Except he pulled it in three separate withdrawals, from three different branches, on three straight days, each one just under the amount that gets a teller's attention.
That's not panic. That's somebody who read the rules first.
Four names on the contacts page. All four checked out in one afternoon. Real cases have dead ends. This folder didn't have one. Grief's messy. This wasn't grief.
Yeah, Voss used to come in Thursdays. Stopped about a month back. Didn't say why. Quiet guy.
He seem worried last time you saw him? Scared, anything like that?

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — a little too rehearsed
dialogueBeats.text: No, actually. Real calm. Like a guy who already made up his mind about something.

"Already made up his mind." That's a strange thing for a bartender to remember word for word about a guy who stopped showing up a month ago. That's not a memory. That's a line somebody handed him and told him to have ready.
Third night on it and I'm still building a case out of paper. The answer was across a diner table Tuesday. Paper doesn't stand up and leave.
One in the morning. Either David Voss vanished clean, or somebody built me a map. Every road led where she wanted me standing. Some part of me still wanted it to be the first one.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — alert, present tense now. A car outside, slowing
dialogueBeats.text: Noticed the car because it did something none of Solomon's guys had bothered doing yet. It parked.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — lower, wary. A car door closing soft, not slammed
dialogueBeats.text: Slammed doors, I can work with. Amateurs slam doors. It's the quiet ones you gotta watch.

dialogueBeats.expression: calling out, keeping his voice steady
dialogueBeats.text: Bit late for company.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — the last clear thought before it all goes sideways
dialogueBeats.text: And that's about when I remembered I'd left my gun in the car. Which, for the record, is not a mistake I usually make twice in one lifetime.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — fading, disoriented, cutting off mid-thought
dialogueBeats.text: Somebody hit me with something a lot heavier than a hand. Floor came up faster than it should've. Last clear thought I had before the lights went out — I never asked what David Voss looked like. Three days on the case. That's not an oversight.

action.text: Six grand, three withdrawals, three branches, three days — each just under the amount that gets a teller's attention.
Four names. All four checked out in one afternoon. Real cases have dead ends. This folder didn't have one.

scenes.title: Part 4 — The Man Who Curates Debts
scenes.prose: Zip-tied to a metal chair. Cold concrete. Motor oil, old rain.

dialogueBeats.text: Warehouse. Shipping crates stacked to the ceiling, one bare bulb doing all the work. And sitting across from me in a folding chair — like he'd brought it from home — was a man I'd only ever heard about secondhand.
One moment, Mr. Morrow. I'm finishing something.

dialogueBeats.expression: quick, panicked, mid-forties, trying to sound reasonable
dialogueBeats.text: I've got it Friday. I swear to God I've got it Friday, I've got hours coming —
Ted. I know. I'm not here about Friday.
Then—

dialogueBeats.expression: the sound of paper being slid across
dialogueBeats.text: Your daughter turned eighteen in March. She's on the account now. That's just how the paper works when a co-signer ages in — I didn't do it, the form did it. I wanted you to hear it from me and not find out at a bank.

dialogueBeats.expression: barely — a small, wrecked sound. Not a sob. Worse. Comprehension.
dialogueBeats.text: She's got a job in Fairview. She was gonna —
I know. And Friday's still Friday. Nothing's changed today, Ted. I just don't like people being surprised.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, cold. Ted walked out. A door. Silence.
dialogueBeats.text: He didn't threaten him. He didn't raise his voice. He showed a man a piece of paper that moved his debt onto his kid, and then he told him it wasn't personal because a form did it. That's what he is. Not a man with a gun. A man with a filing system that eats people slowly and lets him feel administrative about it.
Mr. Morrow. Sorry about the chair. My guys have a flair for the dramatic I've never managed to train out of them.
You're Solomon Reyes.
I am. And you've been asking my people about a man who owes me money. I'd like to know why.
Client hired me to find her husband. That's the whole job. I didn't know he owed you anything till two nights ago.
I believe you. That's actually the problem.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let him cut you loose.

action.text: A coffee ring on it. A filing system that eats people slowly and lets him feel administrative about it.
Like he'd brought it from home. Surprise buys you about four good seconds — the chair was all you needed.

scenes.title: Part 4 — The Man Who Curates Debts
scenes.prose: The bare bulb doing all the work. The hum. Dripping water somewhere.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — dry, narrating over a lighter flicking open
dialogueBeats.text: Most guys who kidnap you lead with a threat. This one led with "I believe you," which somehow scared me more, because it meant he was actually thinking, not just posturing.

David Voss owed me money. Then he disappeared. Then a detective shows up asking my people questions about him like he thinks he's looking for a missing husband. I don't think that's what you're looking for anymore. I think somebody's using you to find my money.

dialogueBeats.expression: measured, and honestly tired of pretending otherwise
dialogueBeats.text: Yeah. That's about where I landed too.

dialogueBeats.expression: quieter, almost curious — standing, circling the chair slowly
dialogueBeats.text: Then we understand each other. I don't actually care about David Voss. Guys who run from me save me the trouble of deciding what to do with them. What I care about is the money. And right now you're the only piece of this I didn't put there myself.

dialogueBeats.expression: wry, pushing his luck because it's the only thing he's got left
dialogueBeats.text: You always talk this much before you let a guy go, or is tonight special?

scenes.title: Part 4 — The Man Who Curates Debts
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 4 — The Man Who Curates Debts
scenes.prose: Footsteps stopping directly behind the chair. Silence.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat, no warmth left at all. Footsteps stopping directly behind the chair.
dialogueBeats.text: Who said I was letting you go.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — low, urgent, all business now
dialogueBeats.text: He left two guys on me. Not Moe and Desh — a different pair, less interested in grocery store conspiracy theories, more interested in standing near the exit. Which worked out fine for me. Standing still near an exit tells you exactly where the exit is.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — focused, straining against the zip tie
dialogueBeats.text: Felt around behind me. Metal chair, cheap bolts, one of 'em loose enough to work at if I had a week to spare, which I didn't. Then my knuckle caught something sharp on the floor — a piece of that lamp, still in my coat pocket from two nights back, when somebody'd introduced my head to it. Small mercy. Sharp edges make good friends when your hands are tied.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet, breathless. A soft snap.
dialogueBeats.text: Zip tie gave before my patience did. Close race, though.
He's loose! Get the fuck up—

I'm not a young man, and I've never once won a fight I planned ahead of time. But surprise buys you about four good seconds. Four seconds was all I needed to get a hand on the folding chair Solomon left behind.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — wincing. A metal chair connecting with something solid.
dialogueBeats.text: One down. One left, and this one skipped the fists and went straight for a gun.

dialogueBeats.expression: shouting, adrenaline in the voice. A gunshot ricocheting off metal.
dialogueBeats.text: I would've settled for the four fucking seconds!

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — breathless, quick. A heavy door bursting open; rain and empty-street silence flooding in.
dialogueBeats.text: Knocked a crate into his path. Didn't hit him, but it bought me the door, which was really all I was asking for.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — out of breath, running. Made it two blocks. Made it four. A payphone.
dialogueBeats.text: Made it two blocks before my legs reminded me I'm forty-four and this is not a young man's line of work. Made it four before I stopped hearing footsteps behind me. Made it all the way to a payphone — real one, still worked, God bless whoever forgot to rip it out — before I actually let myself think about what Solomon Reyes had told me.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, standing in the rain before dialing
dialogueBeats.text: He didn't care about David Voss. Meant it. Which meant somebody else did — enough to build me a folder and let me walk in blind. I stood in the rain a long time before I dialed.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — groggy, half-asleep, immediately sharpening
dialogueBeats.text: Morrow? It's two in the morning. This better be good.

dialogueBeats.expression: cutting her off, low and urgent
dialogueBeats.text: Rosa. I need you to run David Voss for me. Cards, bus depots, motel registries — anything that moved. And I need you to not ask how I got tangled up in this yet.
I didn't have an answer for her either. I knew whoever sent me into that warehouse wasn't finished. First time I wondered if I wanted her to be who I hoped she was.

choices.text: Hang up. Stand in the rain a minute.

scenes.title: Part 4 (alt) — The Offer
scenes.prose: The bare bulb. The hum. Dripping water somewhere.

dialogueBeats.expression: direct — a beat before the last two sentences
dialogueBeats.text: David Voss owed me money. Then he disappeared. Then a detective shows up asking my people questions about him. I don't think you're looking for a missing husband. I think somebody's using you to find my money.
That's about where I landed too.
Solomon standing. Footsteps circling the chair.
Then let me save us both a fortnight.
The zip tie being cut. Jack's arms coming free. He doesn't move.
Find him. Same job. Same man. Two hundred a day, which I understand is your rate, and a number at the end of it that I won't insult you by naming yet.
I've got a client.
You've got a client who hasn't told you what she's paying you to find. I've told you inside four minutes. Consider which of us is being straight with you.
An envelope set on the arm of the folding chair. Not slid. Placed.
I'm not asking you to drop her. Keep her. Take her money. All I want is to be told at the same time she is. Not before. At the same time.
A long silence. The bare bulb. Water dripping somewhere.

scenes.title: Part 4 (alt) — The Offer
scenes.partBreak: Act One, Part 4 (alt) — The Offer
scenes.prose: The envelope picked up. A long silence. The bare bulb.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'carrying around'
dialogueBeats.text: Sixteen years. That's the number I'd been carrying around like it meant something. It took four minutes and a folding chair.
Good. That's sensible.
It's not sensible. It's just easier.

dialogueBeats.expression: a small nod — a beat after 'Yes'
dialogueBeats.text: Yes. Most sensible things are. People get very confused about that.
Jack standing. Unsteady. The chair scraping.

dialogueBeats.expression: as Jack reaches the door, conversational
dialogueBeats.text: Mr. Morrow. One thing.
What.
In 2015 there was a file with my name in it and a young detective who was asked twice to lose it, and wouldn't.
Rain outside. The bulb humming.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, and it isn't cruelty — it's disappointment
dialogueBeats.text: I'd like you to know I'm sorry to have finally met him.
A heavy door. Rain. Footsteps on wet ground, not running.
I walked four blocks with an envelope in my coat and I did not once think about giving it back. I thought about what I'd spend it on. That's the true version.

endingData.headline: END OF ACT ONE
endingData.recap: He didn't care about David Voss — he cared about the money, and somebody used you to go looking for it. Rosa's running the name. The rain hasn't stopped once.

scenes.prose: So I followed her home. END OF ACT ONE.

endingData.headline: THREE WEEKS
endingData.recap: You said no, and you were right, and being right didn't stop a single thing. Three weeks later: the same booth, the same time, and a town that kept happening without you.

scenes.prose: I did the sensible thing and I felt sensible about it for about four days. END OF ACT ONE.

endingData.headline: SHE'S NOT ANSWERING
endingData.recap: You said her name in a pool hall to watch a man blink, and his face stayed exactly where it was. Solomon knows where she is now. Nineteen hours is all she had.

scenes.prose: Nineteen hours. That's how long she had, and I gave it away in a pool hall, for free. END OF ACT ONE.

endingData.headline: TWO ENVELOPES

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — Past Tense
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — Past Tense
scenes.prose: A residential street in Blackwood. Rain. An engine off. A car interior — Jack parked, waiting. Vera's house across the road, one light on upstairs.

dialogueBeats.text: I asked her what he looked like. Three days on a missing persons case, it's the first question you ask. I'd gone a whole conversation without it.
Rain on the roof.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, stressing 'was' and 'had' — a beat before the last two sentences
dialogueBeats.text: She said: he was about six foot. He had a scar through one eyebrow. Nobody talks about a missing husband in the past tense. They talk about him like he's late.
A door opening across the street. Footsteps.
So I didn't open the folder. I sat outside her house instead, which is the sort of thing that costs you your licence, and I watched her carry two bags of shopping in at eleven at night.
A car door. Bags. A door closing.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet — a beat after 'One woman'
dialogueBeats.text: Two bags. One woman. Everybody buys too much sometimes. I wrote it down anyway, and I hated myself a bit for writing it down, and I've since been very glad I did.
Rain. A long hold.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'go home'
dialogueBeats.text: I should have called Rosa that night. She'd have told me to go home. That's why I didn't.

choices.text: Stand in the rain a moment.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — The Route Somebody's Drawn
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — The Route Somebody's Drawn
scenes.prose: Jack's office. Morning. Rain easing. The folder, unopened, exactly where he left it.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'doesn't sleep either'
dialogueBeats.text: I sat outside her house till about four and learned nothing except that she doesn't sleep either. Then I went home, and I woke up at eleven, and the folder was still on the desk being patient.
An envelope opening. Paper.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'four answers'
dialogueBeats.text: Everything in it checked out inside an afternoon. Four names, four calls, four answers. That's not a case. That's a route somebody's drawn.
Papers. A pen tapping once.
The bit she didn't draw was a utility bill. Rental four hours north, weekly rate, paid cash — and the power switched on in his own name because a man who's cold stops being clever.
A chair. Keys.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'stay put'
dialogueBeats.text: I could have rung Rosa. She'd have run it properly and told me to stay put. I'd spent the night outside my own client's house. I wasn't ringing anybody.

endingData.headline: FOUR HOURS NORTH
endingData.recap: Everything in it checked out inside an afternoon — four names, four calls, four answers. That's not a case. That's a route somebody's drawn. The utility bill pointed at a rental: weekly, cash, power on in his own name.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — Two Envelopes
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — Two Envelopes
scenes.prose: Jack's office, morning. Rain. Papers. A kettle somewhere. Two envelopes on the desk — one manila, worn soft at the corners, Vera's folder. One plain white, thicker, unopened.

dialogueBeats.text: He didn't threaten me. That's worth saying. He offered me a job, at a rate, in writing, like a man who's never had to do it the other way because the other way is slower.
An envelope being picked up. Set down again.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'the other'
dialogueBeats.text: Find David Voss. Same job. Same man. Two clients, and neither of them told the other. I've taken worse and slept fine.
Rain on the window.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'explain and can't'
dialogueBeats.text: Here's the part I'd like to explain and can't. I took it because it was easier to hold both than to pick. Sixteen years of not working for that man, and it went in one morning, for money, before anybody had even died.
A chair. A long silence.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet — a beat after 'give the money back after'
dialogueBeats.text: I told myself I'd give the money back after. I want to be clear that I did tell myself that.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — On Two Salaries
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — On Two Salaries
scenes.prose: Jack's office. The two envelopes. Rain.

dialogueBeats.text: Two clients want the same man found. That's not a conflict, that's efficiency. I told myself that at about nine in the morning and it held up till roughly lunchtime.
Papers. A phone picked up, dialled, ringing.
It's been a while.
I need an address off a utility account. Four hours north.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — a pause, he's heard something in it
dialogueBeats.text: Who's asking, Jack.
A beat. Rain.
Me.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — after a moment
dialogueBeats.text: Right.
The call ending.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'down a phone line'
dialogueBeats.text: He knew. Doc's sold to Solomon's people twice this year and he could hear it on me down a phone line. That's what it sounds like from the outside, apparently. I'd always wondered.
Keys. A door.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'the person he's hiding from'
dialogueBeats.text: Four hours north, on two salaries, to find a man for the person he's hiding from. I drove it at the speed limit the whole way. Felt like the last decent thing available.

endingData.headline: ON TWO SALARIES
endingData.recap: Two clients, one man, and Doc Sato heard it on you down a phone line. You drove four hours north on two salaries — at the speed limit the whole way, felt like the last decent thing available.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — Three Weeks
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — Three Weeks
scenes.prose: The Blackwood Diner. Rain. The ceiling fan. Same as always. The same booth, the same time. Jack alone, coffee cold. Nothing has changed, and that's the horror of it.

dialogueBeats.text: I said no. I want you to know it's possible. She sat down, she made her case, and I looked at the shape of it and I said no thank you, Mrs. Voss, and she picked up her folder and left.
The fan. Rain.
Best decision I ever made. I've had three weeks to enjoy it.
A bell — the door. Footsteps, heavier than Vera's. A booth creaking.
They found a man in a rental four hours north. Nine days dead.
Okay.
His wife came to see you three weeks ago.
Rain. The fan.
She did.
And you said no.
I said no.
A long silence.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after 'your friend' and after 'anywhere'
dialogueBeats.text: I need you to understand something, Jack. I'm not here as your friend. You're the last person she spoke to about him before he went, and you've got no client, no notes, and no reason to have been anywhere. That's not innocent. That's just unhelpful.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'it's worse'
dialogueBeats.text: Turns out there's a version where you do the smart thing and it's worse. I hadn't accounted for that one.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — Off the Record
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — Off the Record
scenes.prose: The Blackwood Diner. The fan. Rosa still opposite him.

dialogueBeats.text: They've got him as a robbery. Rental four hours north, cash on the premises, gone.
You don't think it's a robbery.
I think there's a version where I hand this to the state boys and go home at six.
The fan. Rain.
That's the address. It's not sealed yet. Nobody's been through the place properly.
You're giving me a crime scene.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after 'say no to her'
dialogueBeats.text: I'm giving you the last place a man was alive, and I'm doing it because you're the only person in this county who was smart enough to say no to her, and I want to know what you see. Off the record. Permanently off the record.
A long pause.
And if I find something.
Then we'll both have a problem we didn't have this morning.
Three weeks of being right, and it took her four minutes to get me in the car anyway.

endingData.headline: PERMANENTLY OFF THE RECORD
endingData.recap: Three weeks of being right, and it took Rosa four minutes to get you in the car. The rental is a crime scene now — cash on the premises, gone. Off the record. Permanently.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — She's Not Answering
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 1 — She's Not Answering
scenes.prose: A phone ringing out. Ring. Ring. Ring. No answer. It goes on too long. Jack's office, the folder open, his phone on the desk on speaker, ringing into nothing.

dialogueBeats.text: I said her name in a bar. That's all I did. Two men who'd told me they'd never heard of David Voss, and I handed them the wife.
The ringing stops. Voicemail tone.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'Nineteen hours'
dialogueBeats.text: Nineteen hours. That's how long it took. I've done this job sixteen years and I have never once given a client's name to the other side, and I did it in a pool hall because I wanted to see a man's face change.
The phone being redialled. Ringing again.
It didn't change. That's the part that stays with me. Moe heard the name and nothing happened in his face at all, and I remember thinking I'd got away with it.
Ringing. Ringing. Then — picked up. Silence on the line. Not Vera's breathing.
Mr. Morrow. She's fine. I want to say that first because I know what you're about to think.
Rain. Jack not speaking.
You've saved us all a great deal of time. I'd like to thank you properly, and I'd like you to come here and let me do it.

scenes.title: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — She's Upstairs
scenes.partBreak: Act Two (alt), Part 2 — She's Upstairs
scenes.prose: The feed store office. The space heater. Rain on one window.

dialogueBeats.text: She's upstairs. She's had a cup of tea and she's extremely angry with you, which I'd say is proportionate.
Let me see her.

dialogueBeats.expression: mild — a beat after 'In a while'
dialogueBeats.text: In a while. You've given me a name I didn't have, Mr. Morrow, and I'd like to be fair about that, so I'm going to give you one back.
Paper. A single sheet slid across a desk.

dialogueBeats.expression: mild — a beat after 'his own name'
dialogueBeats.text: Rental four hours north. Weekly, cash. The power's on in his own name. I've had it since Tuesday.
Then why haven't you—

dialogueBeats.expression: cutting in, unbothered — a beat after 'He's just found'
dialogueBeats.text: Because a man who's found isn't finished. He's just found. I'd like him to be told, by somebody he'll believe, that his wife is sat in a room above a feed store. And then I'd like to see what he does.
A long silence. The heater.
So that's the job now. Drive four hours and be the worst news a man's ever had, and do it well, because she's upstairs.

endingData.headline: SHE'S UPSTAIRS
endingData.recap: Solomon had the address since Tuesday — and she's upstairs, a cup of tea, extremely angry with you. Drive four hours and be the worst news a man's ever had. And do it well.

scenes.title: Act Two, Part 1 — Nobody Just Leaves
scenes.partBreak: Act Two, Part 1 — Nobody Just Leaves
scenes.prose: Rain easing to a drizzle. An all-night laundromat hum, a dryer tumbling somewhere in the background. Rosa doesn't like meeting this late. Says it makes her feel like a source instead of a cop. Tonight she was.

dialogueBeats.expression: sitting down across from him, arms crossed, worry underneath the annoyance
dialogueBeats.text: You look like hell, Morrow.
You should see the other guy. Actually you should see the other two guys. I left them in a warehouse.
That's not funny.
Wasn't trying to be.

dialogueBeats.expression: serious now, direct — setting a folded printout on the table
dialogueBeats.text: I ran the name you gave me. David Voss. You want the short version or the long version?
Short version. I've had a long night.
Short version — he's not missing. Not the way your client's telling it, anyway.
What do you mean?

Nine days ago he bought a bus ticket out of the Blackwood depot. Cash. But he used his own card at a motel four hours north the same night, and the clerk remembers him because he tipped. Nobody kidnaps a man and lets him tip a motel clerk, Jack. He walked onto that bus on his own two feet.
She told me three weeks missing. That leaves almost two weeks he was sitting somewhere in this country before he ever left it.
Which means either he was hiding domestic first and got spooked into leaving the country — or somebody's timeline is off on purpose.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. A dryer buzzer going off somewhere in the background.
dialogueBeats.text: There it was. What I'd been circling for two days. Landing on it meant admitting something about myself too.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat, and it costs him something to say it
dialogueBeats.text: You think my client already knew he left on his own.
Town this size, a woman wants her husband found, she asks around. Two days, she knows. She doesn't hire a detective.
Meaning.

Meaning hiring you isn't looking for him. It's a record of having looked. I'm not saying she's lying about everything. I'm saying you built her a story where she's the victim, and some part of you needed her to be.
Yeah. Probably.
I'm not trying to hurt you with this.
I know. That's kind of the problem. You're the only one who isn't.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, folding the printout, tucking it into his coat
dialogueBeats.text: I'd built that story out of one good line in a diner. Now I believed it. Just not the way she meant it.
I need to find him. Not her version of him. The real one.
Then you do it careful. If Solomon's people already grabbed you once, they're not gonna be polite about a second time.

dialogueBeats.expression: half a smile, already heading for the door
dialogueBeats.text: When have I ever been polite about a first time.

dialogueBeats.expression: calling after him, exasperated but caring
dialogueBeats.text: Jack—

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The door chime, rain picking back up.
dialogueBeats.text: She didn't finish the sentence. Didn't need to. Six years she's been saying some version of it. Never once wrong.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet, determined. Wipers starting; the engine pulling away.
dialogueBeats.text: But now I had a motel four hours north and a clerk who remembered a man who tipped. First real lead in this whole case that hadn't been handed to me on somebody else's paper. Time to find out where a man goes when nobody's chasing him.

action.text: Nobody at this hour but the two of you and somebody's laundry going around. A buzzer goes off. Nobody comes for it.

scenes.title: Part 1b — Three in the Morning
scenes.partBreak: Act Two, Part 1b — Three in the Morning
scenes.prose: Jack's office. Late. A desk lamp. Rain on the window. Papers. No music. The only scene in the film where they are not adversaries. Nothing happens. That's the point — it's the scene the ending spends.

dialogueBeats.text: Three in the morning. Didn't call first. Nobody does here. Phones work, people stopped expecting them to.
Your light was on.
My light's always on.
I know. I've driven past it.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. She comes in. A chair.
dialogueBeats.text: I want to be accurate here. She didn't work me. She sat in a bad chair and asked what I was doing.
What are you doing.
Your husband's bank statements. Third time through.
Why three times?
Because I'm good at this and it's the only thing I've been good at for a decade and I don't have anywhere to be.
Show me.
Show you what?
What you see when you look at it. Nobody's ever shown me what they're good at. Everyone here does one thing badly for money.

dialogueBeats.expression: warming, absorbed — the most alive he sounds in the film
dialogueBeats.text: Three withdrawals. Three branches. Three days.
What's that mean.
Everybody sees that and thinks nervous. It's not nervous. Nervous is one big one and a plane ticket. This is somebody who did the homework. Careful people leave a different shape than scared people.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, watching him rather than the page
dialogueBeats.text: What shape do I leave?

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The lamp buzzing. He doesn't answer.
dialogueBeats.text: That was the whole thing. Four seconds to answer it correctly. I let it sit until it stopped being a question.
Sorry. That was — ignore that.
No, it wasn't.
Do you like it here?
Nobody likes it here.
That's not what I asked.

I know every road in this town. Which houses have somebody in them. What the mill sounded like when it ran — there's maybe eleven hundred of us left who do. Not liking it. Not nothing either. Only thing Blackwood gives you, and it gives it free.
And you'd stay.
Nobody's ever asked me to be anywhere else.

dialogueBeats.expression: carefully, and she starts something she doesn't finish
dialogueBeats.text: Jack. If I told you—

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The desk phone ringing. Loud. Wrong. Shattering it.
dialogueBeats.text: Wrong number, maybe. Rang four times. By the time it stopped she'd put it away. I watched her put it away. Didn't ask.
It's late. You've got a drive tomorrow.
Vera.
Find him. That's what I'm paying for.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The door. Her car starting outside, pulling away. The office. The lamp. Rain. Jack not moving.
dialogueBeats.text: Sat there another hour. Didn't work. Tried to guess what she'd been about to say, then decided — the way a man decides on a second drink — that I didn't want to know badly enough to ask.
Last hour of my life nobody was dead yet. I spent it not asking a question.

endingData.headline: THREE IN THE MORNING
endingData.recap: Rosa ran the name — bus ticket, cash, nine days ago. He wasn't taken, he walked. And at three in the morning, nothing happened. That's the point.

action.text: One lamp, buzzing. Two heads bent over the same page in one pool of lamplight — the closest they get to each other in the whole film.

scenes.title: Part 2 — Forty-Eight Hours
scenes.partBreak: Act Two, Part 2 — Forty-Eight Hours
scenes.prose: Jack's car engine idling, rain on the windshield, a phone buzzing on the dashboard. Hadn't made the parking lot before my phone went off. Number I didn't know. Never a coupon.

dialogueBeats.text: Four hours north. The address is on a slip of paper Rosa slid across a diner table, and the whole trip runs on that: no client, no clock, no reason except that a man's been dead nine days and the county's already made up the story.
Rosa mentioned the motel on the way. One night, cash rate, nine days back. She didn't say how she'd got it. She never says how she gets things.
I wasn't racing a clock. I keep coming back to that, later. I was driving four hours toward a house with the power on in his own name, and I couldn't have told you what I was hoping to find in it.

Four hours north. No client, no clock, no case. Just an address on a single sheet of paper in a feed-store typeface, and a sentence a man said over a phone: I'd like him to be told, by somebody he'll believe, that his wife is sat in a room above a feed store.

I've done this job sixteen years, and delivering the worst news is not in it, and I made sure of that. Turns out it gets in anyway, when you give a name to a room full of a man's people to watch whether a face changes.
The road north is two lanes wide and it's still raining. I wasn't racing a clock. I was driving toward a kitchen where a man was making tea.
Yeah.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — calm, almost friendly
dialogueBeats.text: Mr. Morrow. Glad you made it out of the warehouse. Genuinely. I'd have hated to lose you before we finished our conversation.
Didn't realize we were still having one.

We are now. You've got forty-eight hours to bring me David Voss or my money. I don't especially care which. After that, I stop being patient, and I start being thorough. You understand the difference?

dialogueBeats.expression: dry, masking how rattled he is
dialogueBeats.text: Thorough sounds worse.
It is. Forty-eight hours, Mr. Morrow.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The call disconnecting. Tires on wet pavement, the car accelerating.
dialogueBeats.text: A clock. Loud enough to hear over the rain.

First stop was the motel paperwork Rosa couldn't legally hand me but somehow ended up in my glove compartment anyway. One night, cash rate, nine days back. Four hours north — far enough that nobody from Blackwood would wander through, close enough he could still get home if he lost his nerve. That's not a man escaping. That's a man waiting for somebody.
It's me. I need a favor and I need it in the next hour, not the next day.
Everybody needs everything in the next hour. What makes you special?
Because if I don't have a name and an address by sundown, a very patient man's gonna stop being patient, and I've already met his idea of not patient once this week.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — a beat, then more serious
dialogueBeats.text: Send me what you've got. I'll see what I can pull.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. Engine noise swelling, rain intensifying.
dialogueBeats.text: Forty-eight hours sounds like a lot until you do the math. Four just to drive up. Solomon's people had the same motel clerk I did. They could pay him better.

I wasn't the only one racing that clock. Just the only one hoping it meant something good for somebody. Four hours north. A man who wasn't missing, about to find out how little disappearing well was going to save him.

choices.text: Two hours north. Stop for gas.

action.text: Motel paperwork Rosa couldn't legally hand me. Somehow it ended up in here anyway. One night, cash rate, nine days back.
A slip of paper in the glove compartment. An address in Rosa's handwriting, nothing else. Off the record. Permanently.
A single sheet in the glove compartment. An address in typeface, nothing else. Four hours north, and the power on in his own name, and the man who wrote it pleased about it.

scenes.title: Part 2b — The Pumps at Route 6
scenes.partBreak: Act Two, Part 2b — The Pumps at Route 6
scenes.prose: A gas station off a two-lane road. Wind. A pump ticking. A radio inside playing something country and badly tuned. Fluorescent buzz. Two men on a bench by the ice machine. Nothing here advances the plot. That's the point.

dialogueBeats.expression: mid-rant, not the start of it
dialogueBeats.text: —eleven years, Denny. Eleven fucking years, and she's out the door with a bloke who sells hot tubs.
Hot tubs is decent money.
That is not the fucking point.
It's a bit of the point.
It is not a bit of the point, you daft bastard. The point is she's a lying, cheating bitch who had a whole other phone.
Ah. There it is.
A whole other phone. In the glovebox. Under the manual. Who the fuck reads the manual, Denny? Nobody. That's not a hiding place, that's a decision.
That's the bit that gets you.
That's exactly the bit that gets me.
Not the bloke.
Fuck the bloke. The bloke's an idiot with a van. It's the filing. She had a system, Denny. She had a system and I was inside it.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, quiet. His pump clicking off. He doesn't move to hang it up.
dialogueBeats.text: Two hours north. Stopped at a place with three pumps and one that worked. I'd been in my own head a hundred miles and I was glad of the noise. That lasted about forty seconds.
Can I say something.
Say it.
You knew.
I did not fucking know.
Gary. Four months back you asked me if it was normal for a woman to start doing her hair on a Tuesday.
That's not knowing.
That's the exact shape of knowing. That's knowing with a fucking hat on.

dialogueBeats.expression: quieter. Wind. The radio inside, badly tuned.
dialogueBeats.text: I asked you because I wanted you to tell me it was normal.
I know. That's why I said it was normal.
That was a shit thing to do, Denny.
It was, yeah.

dialogueBeats.expression: eventually. The ice machine cycling. Wind.
dialogueBeats.text: What'd you want me to say?

dialogueBeats.expression: honest, and this is the only quiet thing he says
dialogueBeats.text: Nothing. That's the hell of it, isn't it. There's no version where you say it and I hear it. You'd have said it and I'd have had a different bloke to be angry at for four months, and she'd still have been in the glovebox.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet. Hanging up the nozzle. The clunk of it.

dialogueBeats.text: Alright.
Alright.

dialogueBeats.expression: gesturing at Gary with the paper bag
dialogueBeats.text: Don't mind him. He's having a year.
Yeah. Me too.
You married?
No.
Smart man.
It's not that.
Because here's the thing nobody fucking tells you. You think it's going to be a moment. Door slamming, suitcase, all that. It's not. It's a Tuesday, and she does her hair, and you decide not to ask.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, quiet. The pump ticking. Wind. Jack not moving.
dialogueBeats.text: Bloke at a petrol station in the middle of nowhere, eating out of a paper bag, and he'd got the whole thing in one sentence. It's a Tuesday and you decide not to ask.
Drive safe.
Yeah.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The door shutting. The engine. Gravel. The forecourt light receding.
dialogueBeats.text: I got about six miles before I had to pull over. Not for anything. I just couldn't be doing seventy toward her with that sentence in the car.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — very quiet. An engine idling on a hard shoulder. Wind. Nothing else.
dialogueBeats.text: Four months, that bloke said. I've had nine days and I've been better at it than he ever was.

action.text: Three pumps and one that worked. Moths going at the light. The nozzle clicks off and he doesn't hang it up.

hotspots.label: The bench by the ice machine

action.text: Two men. One having a year. The other telling him the exact shape of knowing with a hat on.

scenes.title: Interlude — What She Carries
scenes.prose:
A smaller place. Warmer light than anywhere else in this story has had. She's not performing for anyone. No one's watching. That's the point.

A shoebox: photographs, handwritten in the margins. A man's watch, stopped, the leather band cracked with age. She holds it a long moment — the way you hold something you're afraid of dropping and afraid of letting go of at the same time.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — quiet, almost spoken rather than sung, barely audible
dialogueBeats.text: He used to say the debt wasn't the money. Said the money's just what they hand you a bill for. The debt's what you owe the people who trusted you before any of this started.

scenes.title: Part 3 — The Plan Nobody Told Me About
scenes.partBreak: Act Two, Part 3 — The Plan Nobody Told Me About
scenes.prose: A quiet residential street. Crickets. Much less rain here than Blackwood. Rental, dead-end street, weekly, cash, under a name that isn't David Voss.

dialogueBeats.expression: the duffel bags by the door
state tape across the door, sagging in the rain. Two men inside. They let him through.

dialogueBeats.text: Nine days. The clock on the wall is still running. That's the thing nobody puts in a file — a house keeps its time anyway.

dialogueBeats.expression: the kitchen. Crickets outside. Quiet — deliberately, unbearably ordinary.
V.O. — flat. Moving through, not searching. Reading it.
dialogueBeats.text: Two duffel bags, gone. One of them never opened. A cup by the sink, full, never drunk — the kind of ordinary that takes a while to look at.

Cash on the premises, gone. That's the robbery. A man who moved two-eleven across a state line in a bag doesn't get robbed for the change. Somebody dressed this house in a story, and the story's already on the radio.

dialogueBeats.expression: inside the cupboard, under a shelf that was supposed to hold flour — a list

dialogueBeats.text: Six tables. Bread in the morning. Two words under both, in pencil: patient. I stood there a long time with a dead man's list, and I didn't know which of us it was for.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The door. The yard.
dialogueBeats.text: On the way out the state radio was doing it again. Robbery, cash on the premises, gone. I let it play. Some stories get to be true the first time they're told.

dialogueBeats.expression: the chain rattling loose. A kitchen with the kettle ticking as it cools. Two mugs on the counter.
wary, not looking at the door
dialogueBeats.text: Morrow. She sent you. It's late.
Sorry about the hour.
Make it quick. The neighbours notice cars.

dialogueBeats.expression: a second mug put out, then put back in the cupboard. Rain starting out here.

dialogueBeats.text: Solomon's got your wife in a room above the feed store.

dialogueBeats.expression: a long hold. The kettle. Rain.

dialogueBeats.text: Right. I'll bring it back.
Not a beat. Not a thought. Two hundred and eleven thousand dollars, fourteen months, everything he'd built — right, I'll bring it back. Like he'd been waiting nine days for a reason to.
One thing, since you're telling her anything. The money. The bag. The plan — it was the two of us, all of it.

dialogueBeats.expression: headlights sweeping the window. Tires on gravel. Unhurried.

dialogueBeats.text: That's not your car.
No.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The door. The yard.
dialogueBeats.text: A motel receipt under the sugar bowl. One night, cash, nine days back. The clerk had written 'tipped' in the margin, which is the kind of thing you only write down if it's the kind of thing you remember. A list taped inside the cupboard. Six tables. Bread in the morning. Two words under both, in pencil: patient.

dialogueBeats.expression: the front door coming in — wood splintering — boots on linoleum

dialogueBeats.text: Doc came through. Power switched on under an account that used to be his. People think changing your name fixes everything. It doesn't fix the part that still pays its bills.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. Knocking. Didn't expect an answer. Got one.
wary, exhausted, a little manic — through the chain
dialogueBeats.text: Whoever you are, I don't have anything worth stealing.
Not here to steal anything. Name's Jack Morrow. Your wife hired me to find you.

dialogueBeats.expression: bitter laugh, but underneath it, real fear — the chain rattling loose
dialogueBeats.text: She hired you? Of course she did. Christ. Come in before somebody sees you standing there.
Two duffel bags, unpacked. Part of him still thought he'd have to run. I know that feeling.

Solomon Reyes grabbed me two nights ago. Zip-tied me to a chair and asked real polite where his money was. Gave me forty-eight hours to bring him you or the cash. That clock's down to about thirty now.
Jesus. He got to you already?
He got to me before I knew what “it” was.

dialogueBeats.expression: conversational, which is worse — moving through the room, not searching. Reading it.
dialogueBeats.text: Weekly rate. Cash. Four hours north — not eight, not a state line, four. And you put the power on under your own account.
I needed heat, it was—

dialogueBeats.expression: cutting through, still not raising his voice
dialogueBeats.text: You've got two hundred and eleven thousand dollars in a bag and you're nine days out. You could be anywhere. You could be somewhere with a different alphabet. Instead you're close enough to drive back in an afternoon, under a name that leaves a trail a bored cop could follow, in a house you're paying for one week at a time.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet. David not answering. The kettle ticking.
dialogueBeats.text: That's not a man hiding, David. Weekly means you don't know how long you'll need it. Close means you want to be findable by exactly one person. You're not running. You're waiting.
Yeah.
Nine days.
Yeah.
David. She's not late.

dialogueBeats.expression: after a long moment, not looking at him
dialogueBeats.text: Say the rest of it.

I don't have to. You switched the power on under your own name so she could find you if she'd lost the address. You've been making yourself easy to reach for nine days. You just didn't think about who else that works for.

dialogueBeats.expression: muffled, wrecked — hands over his face. A long exhale.
dialogueBeats.text: Okay. Okay. Then you already know most of it. Ask me anything you want.
You're gonna think I'm the worst person you ever met.
Client list's pretty competitive this week. Try me.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, relief of finally saying it
dialogueBeats.text: Vera and I planned this together. All of it.
The disappearance.
The money. The bus. Fourteen months skimming off Solomon, small enough he never felt it. I pulled the last of it in one go and got out like we agreed.
How much.
Two-eleven. That's what it cost to leave. People have died in that town over a tenth of it.
I'd said most of it on the walk in. Saying it and hearing it are different jobs.
So she didn't hire me to find you. She hired me to prove she never knew where you went.

That was always the plan. You'd dig, you'd come up empty, you'd tell her — and everybody, cops included — that she genuinely had no idea. Clean alibi. Except you didn't come up empty. You came up here.
Then explain something to me. If this was the plan, why do you look like you're about to fall apart every time somebody knocks on your door?

Because two days ago Vera stopped answering the number only I have. And a plan where you split the money fifty-fifty doesn't usually involve one person going quiet right when the other one's ready to collect his half.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. Crickets outside, a car engine faint in the distance.
dialogueBeats.text: Lined up with something I hadn't wanted to say out loud. A woman with an airtight alibi doesn't need her husband walking around to confirm it. I believed it anyway.
You think she's planning on cutting you out.
I think I've been so busy hiding from Solomon I forgot I should've been hiding from her too.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet. A long silence. Crickets. The kettle.
dialogueBeats.text: Sit down. Tell me all of it, from the start, and don't leave things out to make yourself look better. I've had a week of people editing.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, under the fade. David starting to talk, low.
dialogueBeats.text: He talked forty minutes. Most of it I already had. By the end he'd stopped being frightened. Lighter. Like a man told he could put a bag down.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. The kitchen, quieter now. Two men talking low. Crickets outside.
dialogueBeats.text: That's the one thing I'd take back. Not the six seconds. That. I let him put the bag down.

choices.text: The state radio. The story. Drive back.

action.text: Unpacked. Part of him still thought he'd have to run. Two hundred and eleven thousand dollars, and one bag he never opened.
An ordinary rental kitchen. Two mismatched mugs. A kettle ticking as it cools. Deliberately, unbearably ordinary.
Ticking as it cools. Nobody drinks what's in the cups.
Yellow tape, sagging in the rain. One corner peeling like it's given up earlier than the rest of it.
The list, under a shelf that was supposed to hold flour. Six tables. Bread in the morning. Two words under both, in pencil: patient.
Full. Never drunk. Nobody drinks what's in the cups, and nobody's coming to wash it.

scenes.title: Part 4 — Everything I Already Knew
scenes.partBreak: Act Two, Part 4 — Everything I Already Knew
scenes.prose: The kitchen. Crickets outside. Quiet — deliberately, unbearably ordinary.

dialogueBeats.expression: David's hands wrapped around his cup like it's the only warm thing in the room
the state radio, low through the wall. Boots on gravel going away. Tape at the door, sagging.

dialogueBeats.text: They'd been through the house once. They'd be through it again. The file already had a shape — robbery, cash on the premises, gone — and the shape was going to harden into something with a name in it. I knew the name wasn't the truth.

dialogueBeats.expression: the yard. The kitchen window, dark. Crickets. Rain starting, the way it does out here, like the sky's changed its mind.

dialogueBeats.text: I sat in the grass and did the arithmetic. Nine days, and the house didn't know it was a crime scene. The clock on the wall, the cup by the sink, the list in the cupboard. It was still being a kitchen. That's the part I can't put down.

dialogueBeats.expression: a phone. In his hand. Lit up. Ringing.

dialogueBeats.text: It started to ring. I didn't pick it up. I let it go on.

dialogueBeats.expression: one gunshot. Flat. Close. Not dramatic. It sounds like a door slamming.
nothing. Crickets. Rain starting. No dialogue. No narration.
boots walking away, unhurried, across gravel. Two car doors. An engine. Not fast. Then gone. Crickets.
V.O. — flat, and the flatness is the injury
dialogueBeats.text: I stood in the yard with the rain starting and I did the arithmetic. One sentence. Right, I'll bring it back. I'd given him the reason to say it four hours ago in a pool hall, and he'd used it the second it was useful.

dialogueBeats.expression: a phone buzzing. On and on. Nobody answers it.
easier now, the relief of having told someone
dialogueBeats.text: Can I tell you something stupid?
My week's been full of stupid.
There's a place on Ash Street. Used to be a bakery, before. Ovens are still in it. That's what the money was for. Not a boat. Not — I wanted six tables and bread in the morning.
You know how to bake?
Not even a little. That's the point. Everything I ever got good at, I got good at by lying. I wanted one thing I'd have to be bad at first. One thing I earned by being patient.

dialogueBeats.expression: lighter — then headlights sweeping the window. Tires on gravel.
dialogueBeats.text: Nobody's bought it because nobody in Blackwood's got —
That's not your car.
No.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — nothing. Car doors. Boots on gravel, unhurried. Not running. That's worse.

dialogueBeats.text: Back door. There's a back door—
Go. I'll slow them down.
You don't even know these people—
Go.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, almost embarrassed — stopping half a second in the doorway
dialogueBeats.text: Hey. Thanks for not just handing me over the second you knew. Most guys would've.
Don't thank me yet.

dialogueBeats.expression: the front door coming in — wood splintering — boots on linoleum
shouting, pounding toward the back — a screen door banging open — night air
dialogueBeats.text: DAVID— No, no, no—

dialogueBeats.expression: one gunshot. Flat. Close. Not dramatic. It sounds like a door slamming.
nothing. Crickets. The screen door swinging on its spring, slower and slower, until it stops.
boots walking away, unhurried, across gravel. Two car doors. An engine. Not fast. Then gone. Crickets.
Jack's footsteps on grass. Slow. Stopping. HOLD — ten full seconds. Rain starting. No dialogue. No narration.
a phone buzzing. On and on. Nobody answers it.
