scenes.title: Act Three, Part 1 — The Call
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 1 — The Call
scenes.prose: Rain, steady. Jack still in the yard. State-police radios somewhere behind him, distant, indistinct. He sits on wet grass, knees up, phone lit in his hand — the only light source in frame besides distant emergency strobes, red and blue, unfocused in the rain behind him.

dialogueBeats.text: I let it ring four times. Not because I didn't know I was gonna answer. Because I needed those four rings to remember something before I did.
Six tables. Bread in the morning. One thing he'd have to be bad at first.
Six tables. Bread in the morning. Two words under it, in pencil: patient. I read it in a cupboard four hours north, under a shelf that was supposed to hold flour.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — the phone, still ringing. Then — answered.

dialogueBeats.text: Yeah.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — controlled, but something underneath fraying at the edges
dialogueBeats.text: Jack. Thank God. I've been calling since this morning.
Been a long night.
Have you found him? Please tell me you found him.
They've ruled it a robbery. Nine days of not knowing, and a robbery — I need to hear it from somebody who was in the house.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — low, deciding in real time
dialogueBeats.text: There it was. The exact fork in the road. Tell her everything and watch what her face does. Or hold it back and see what she says next without me steering her there.
I found him.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — a sharp breath
dialogueBeats.text: Where. Is he safe?
How did it happen. Tell me how it happened.

dialogueBeats.expression: rain. Jack not answering. It goes on too long.

dialogueBeats.text: Jack.
I was standing about twenty feet away.
Nine days. I'll say the rest to your face. That's where it has to be said.

dialogueBeats.expression: silence on the line. Not a gasp. Nothing at all.
V.O., filtered, phone — after a long moment, very small
dialogueBeats.text: Okay.
That's it? Okay?
I don't know what the other thing is. Nobody's ever told me one before.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — a long, ragged exhale. Breaking, and it doesn't sound performed anymore.
dialogueBeats.text: Jack, I swear to you—
Don't. Not on the phone. Whatever you're gonna swear to me, you're gonna say it to my face, where I can watch you say it.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O., filtered, phone — a shaky breath
dialogueBeats.text: Okay. Where.
I'll text you an address. One hour.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — final beat, quiet, devastated and clear-eyed at the same time
dialogueBeats.text: I still love her. I want that on the record, whatever happens after this. Knowing what I know now didn't put it out. It just means I'm walking toward her with my eyes open instead of closed. I'm not sure that's braver. I think it might just be sadder.

choices.text: Back south. What he did with it.

action.text: Lit in his hand — the only light in frame besides the strobes. Four rings. He needed all four.

scenes.title: Part 2 — What Rosa Knows
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 2 — What Rosa Knows
scenes.prose: City light reflecting off wet asphalt. A car idling at the curb, engine barely audible. Rosa didn't ask where he'd been. She never does when it's bad. She just opens the door.

dialogueBeats.expression: not looking at him, eyes on the street ahead, calm and cold
dialogueBeats.text: David Voss is dead, Jack. Or he will be by morning. You know that.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat, no argument in him left
dialogueBeats.text: I know that.

dialogueBeats.expression: silence. Just rain on the windshield, wipers moving slow.

dialogueBeats.text: I can bring people in. Real ones. Badges that mean something.
Not yet.
Not yet. Christ, Jack. You keep saying that like there's a version of “yet” where it gets easier.

dialogueBeats.expression: low, looking out his own window, avoiding her eyes
dialogueBeats.text: Maybe there isn't. Doesn't mean I stop trying to find it.
You're protecting her. Still. After all this.
Yeah.
I used to think you were the most honest man I knew, Jack. Turns out you just hadn't met anybody worth lying to yourself about yet.
You wouldn't lose a file for them. Eleven months at an empty desk and you wouldn't do it. I watched you do that. Twenty-six years old. Thought it was the most impressive thing a person could be.
Rosa.
I stayed. You didn't. I've made my peace with which of us was right about that. What I can't work out is how a man who wouldn't bend for the whole department bends this fast for one woman in a diner.

dialogueBeats.expression: quieter, and this is not something she planned to say
dialogueBeats.text: There's a transfer sitting on my captain's desk. County sheriff's, forty minutes from here. Actual budget. Actual backup that shows up. I've been sitting on the paperwork eight months because signing it means admitting I've given up on this place ever being anything else.
Rosa. I didn't know that.

Nobody knows. That's rather the point of not signing it. I sign it, I file it Monday, I'm gone by spring. Simple. Except every time I go to sign it I think about who's left holding the department if I do, and I put the pen down.

If I help you and it goes bad, that transfer doesn't happen. Not because they'd fire me. Because nobody signs off on moving a detective who let a murder walk uninvestigated to protect a friend. I want you to know I've done the arithmetic on that too. I'm not walking into this blind either.
She wasn't wrong. I didn't have anything to say back that wouldn't have made it worse.

dialogueBeats.expression: softer now, almost gentle, which somehow lands harder
dialogueBeats.text: I'm not gonna stop you. I want you to know that. I'm just not gonna help you walk into it blind, either.

dialogueBeats.expression: low, sincere — stepping back out into the rain
dialogueBeats.text: I know what I'm walking into.
No. You know what you're hoping for. That's not the same thing, and you know it.
She was right about that too. I've been doing that a lot lately — hoping instead of knowing, and calling it a plan.

One hour till the address I gave her. I had exactly that long to decide which one I was gonna be when I got there. The man who already knows how this ends. Or the one who still needs to hear her say it.

choices.text: The mill lot. Hear her say it.

action.text: Rain on the glass, wipers moving slow. Two people not looking at each other in a parked car.

scenes.title: Part 3 — Two Hundred and Eleven Thousand
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 3 — Two Hundred and Eleven Thousand
scenes.prose: An empty lot behind the shuttered mill — chain-link, wet gravel, one working sodium light buzzing. Rain fine and constant. No traffic. Nothing.

dialogueBeats.text: I picked the mill lot because nobody comes here. That's not true. Nobody comes here anymore. There's a difference, and in Blackwood it's most of the town.

dialogueBeats.expression: a car pulling in slowly, gravel under tires, engine cutting. A door. Heels on wet stone — not the confident sound from the diner. Slower.

dialogueBeats.text: She didn't bring the coat.
Is he alive?
I don't know.
Is it a robbery.
Okay.
That's it? Okay?
What else is there.
I want to hear you say it. All of it. Out loud, standing there, where I can see your face.
You already know all of it.
Say it anyway.

dialogueBeats.expression: measured, factual — the way people talk about things they've rehearsed alone
dialogueBeats.text: Two hundred and eleven thousand dollars. Fourteen months. David moved it, I tracked it. I picked the date, I built the folder, I picked you.
Why me.
Because you're the only man in Blackwood who doesn't work for Solomon and doesn't want to.
That's not a compliment. That's a spec sheet.
No. It's not a compliment.
Why'd you do it.
Does it matter now?
A man got put in a car in front of me nine hours ago. Yeah. It matters now.
A man's been dead nine days and the county's already got a name for it. Yeah. It matters now.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat, and she volunteers it — he hasn't asked
dialogueBeats.text: I knew Solomon had the address before you did.
Say that again.
Doc Sato sold it to them Tuesday. Six hundred dollars. I found out about eleven hours before you got there. I could have called David. I have the number. I didn't.
Why.

dialogueBeats.expression: not defending it, just answering — a beat after 'willing to lose'
dialogueBeats.text: Because if I called him he'd have run, and if he ran with the money I'd have had nothing, and I hadn't finished deciding what I was willing to lose. I spent eleven hours deciding. That's how long he had, and I spent all of it thinking about myself.
You wanted it out loud. That's the part I'd have left out.

dialogueBeats.expression: smaller, and she doesn't perform any of it
dialogueBeats.text: My father borrowed four thousand dollars from Solomon Reyes. 2011. A furnace.
How much did he end up owing.
Eleven. Nine years and it grew. You don't pay it off here. You pay on it. Forever. Then you hand it to whoever's left.
And that was you.
Kessler. That was my name before David. In case you wondered why Solomon's never once called me Mrs. Voss.
And it came to you.

It came to me at the funeral. Solomon shook my hand at my father's funeral and told me he was sorry for my loss and that we'd talk when I was ready. That's the whole town, Jack. That's Blackwood in one handshake.
He bought that watch for twenty-odd quid, forty years ago. It stopped the winter before he died, and he never did get it fixed — the repair was forty pound, and forty pound was a fortnight.
It's the only thing in that house Solomon never came for. Not because he's decent. Because it's worthless.

dialogueBeats.expression: quieter — a beat after 'I'd ever have'
dialogueBeats.text: So no, I didn't do it for a bag of money. I did it because there's no version of staying here where I ever stop owing him. Not for me. Not for anybody I'd ever have. I wanted out. That's all it ever was. I wanted out and I didn't care what it cost, and then it cost something, and now I care. That's not redemption. That's just arithmetic catching up.
Were you gonna cut him out?

dialogueBeats.expression: the longest silence in the scene
honest, and it's worse than a lie
dialogueBeats.text: I hadn't decided.
Jesus, Vera.
You asked. I'm not going to start lying to you now. That's the one thing I've got left to give you, and it's not worth much.
Tell me how it happened.
No.
Jack—

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, and this is mercy, not cruelty
dialogueBeats.text: No. You get to not have that one. It's the only thing left I can give you and I'm giving it.
He couldn't sleep in a room with the door shut. Since he was a kid. He used to say—

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — spare, devastated — a beat after 'out of her mouth'
dialogueBeats.text: She didn't finish it. Whatever David used to say about doors, she's the only person alive who knew it, and she couldn't get it out of her mouth. That's what it actually is. Not the body. The sentence nobody finishes.
You should go home, Jack.
Not a chance.
I've already cost one man everything he had. I'm standing here doing the math on the second one.
Then stop doing math.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — final beat, spare, no self-pity
dialogueBeats.text: She looked at me for a long time. And I understood, standing in a wet lot behind a mill that closed when I was thirty-two, that she was going to try to save me. That she'd decided it somewhere in the last four seconds, and she was going to be quiet about it, and she was going to be better at it than I was going to be at stopping her.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — very quiet — the sodium light buzzing; a beat after 'tipped a motel clerk'
dialogueBeats.text: He tipped a motel clerk. Nine days ago. Man on the run with two hundred grand in a bag, and he tipped a motel clerk. I keep coming back to that. I don't know why that's the part I can't put down.

choices.text: Call the one person left who'd come.
Why did you talk about him in past tense.

action.text: The same fence from the cold open, wet and out of focus. A single working light behind it.
One working sodium light, buzzing. It's doing all the work. It's the only witness either of them has.
The mill's guts, rusted shut. Four thousand people fed by this, and the place keeps its own silence now.
Parked at the edge of the lot. The boot's shut. In the slant of the sodium light the back seat is empty — no bag, no case. Whatever she's carrying, she's carrying it in herself.

scenes.title: Part 4 — The Cost
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 4 — The Cost
scenes.prose: The mill lot. Rain. Jack alone, standing where he was, for a long moment — then a phone. Two rings. Then, some time later, headlights sweeping the gravel.

dialogueBeats.text: I didn't have a car. Walked here, same as I told you — an hour to think, no vehicle to think in. So I stood in an empty lot behind a dead mill and called the one person left who'd still come get me.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat, covering the silence where a car should be
dialogueBeats.text: Rosa didn't come. The deadline reached me the way everything in this town reaches: secondhand, and late. Friday. Solomon's name on the debt. Two days.

dialogueBeats.expression: a car door opening, closing softly. Rain muffled once inside.
getting in beside him rather than the other way round — she's come to sit with him, not drive off yet
dialogueBeats.text: You told her.
Yeah.
Good. She deserved to hear it from someone who was actually there.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — very quiet. Rain on the windshield. A long silence. The engine still off.
dialogueBeats.text: Twenty minutes before, he was telling me about a building on Ash Street with the ovens still in it.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — very quiet. Rain on the windshield. A long silence. The engine still off.
dialogueBeats.text: The list was inside a cupboard. Six tables. Bread in the morning. The building on Ash Street with the ovens still in it, in a dead man's pencil. He never did get to be bad at anything once.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — barely audible — a beat after 'my words'
dialogueBeats.text: I said "don't thank me yet." Those were my words. I've got the rest of my life to find better ones and it won't matter, because he's not in the room for them.
I never got a word in. Not one. And it turned out the silence was the sentence I spent the rest of the day saying.

dialogueBeats.expression: transition — a car door, engine starting, wipers. Rosa driving. Neither speaks for a while.

dialogueBeats.text: Solomon's put the debt on her. It's formal now. He told two people, which in Blackwood is the same as publishing it.
How much.
All of it. Two-eleven, plus what her father still owed. He's calling it one number now.
That's not a debt. That's a sentence.
Yeah. He knows that. He gave her till Friday.

dialogueBeats.expression: and she says it plainly, because dressing it up would be worse
dialogueBeats.text: The same thing that happened in that house. He's not going to make a speech about it, Jack. It'll just be Friday, and then it'll be Saturday, and she won't be anywhere.
It's Wednesday.
It's Wednesday.
What happens Friday.

dialogueBeats.expression: and she says it plainly, because dressing it up would be worse
dialogueBeats.text: The same thing that happened in that yard. He's not going to make a speech about it, Jack. It'll just be Friday, and then it'll be Saturday, and she won't be anywhere.
She came to see me. Two hours ago.

dialogueBeats.expression: sharp — first real reaction in the scene
dialogueBeats.text: She what?

Walked into the station and asked me what happens to a person who confesses to a theft the victim can't report to the police. She wasn't asking about jail, Jack. She was asking how to make it land on her and nobody else.
She's putting her name on all of it.
She's doing it quiet. She didn't ask me to tell you.
Then why are you.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, and it costs her — Rosa's hands on the wheel, a long pause; a beat after 'found out after'
dialogueBeats.text: Because I've spent three days trying to keep you out of this, and I've lost. So now I'd rather you go in knowing what she's doing than find out after. That's not me helping. That's me giving up. I want you to understand the difference.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, and it costs her — Rosa's hands on the wheel, a long pause; a beat after 'find out after'
dialogueBeats.text: Because I've spent three days trying to keep this off the record, and it's already inside you. So now I'd rather you go in knowing what she's doing than find out after. That's not me helping. That's me giving up. I want you to understand the difference.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after 'Before you called'
dialogueBeats.text: I pulled the transfer paperwork off my captain's desk this morning. Before you called. Not because of you. Because I already knew what I was going to do this week, and there's no version of it that looks good on a form asking whether I've got any active conflicts of interest.
Rosa, don't do that because of me.
I'm not. I'm doing it because of David Voss, same as you. You just get to feel like you're doing it for love. I don't get that part. I just get the paperwork.
I know what that transfer was.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after 'I'm telling you'
dialogueBeats.text: Then you know what I'm telling you. Eight months I couldn't sign it because I didn't want to admit I'd given up on this place. Turns out I didn't give up on the place. I gave up on the form. Same drawer, either way.
Rosa—
Don't. If you say something decent right now I'm going to have to arrest one of you, and I've already decided I'm not going to, and I'd like to keep not deciding that for a few more hours.

dialogueBeats.expression: the car pulling to a stop. Rain.

dialogueBeats.text: That's what it cost her. Not her badge. Her opinion of herself. She handed it over in a parked car in the rain and didn't make me watch her do it.

dialogueBeats.expression: a door opening. Jack getting out. The car idling behind him.
through the open door, last thing
dialogueBeats.text: Jack. Whatever you're about to go do.
Yeah.
Don't tell me about it.

dialogueBeats.expression: the door closing. The car pulling away. Rain on an empty street.

action.text: Rain on the windscreen, the wipers off. Two days of weather between this car and Friday.
Off. She hasn't turned it on. Some silences are a choice.
A paper cup, untouched. She drinks it black. She hasn't touched it since the mill.
A form on the seat, half a page of type, the signature block empty. A transfer request. County sheriff's, forty minutes from here. She's been carrying it in a car she hasn't driven yet.
A red-brick shell going down the road past the mill. Ovens still in it, rusted in their bays. Nobody's bought it. Ash Street.

scenes.title: Part 4b — The Blue Cue, Again
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 4b — The Blue Cue, Again
scenes.prose: The same pool hall. Same warped jukebox. Same balls clacking. Almost identical to Act One — deliberately. Wednesday night. Two days left on her.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — spare, flat — a beat after 'Two days left on her'
dialogueBeats.text: I knew before I opened the door — Blackwood's four thousand people and Solomon keeps two men for the far end of things. There was never going to be anybody else.
— all I'm saying is if the machine can tell it's the wrong item, the machine already knows what the right item is. So why's it asking me?
It's not asking you.
It says "please."
That's not asking. That's a recording of somebody who asked once, in nineteen ninety-whatever, and now it just plays.
Nine days ago I stood in this room and thought that was funny. I want you to understand I laughed. I remember laughing.
Nine days ago I said no in a diner, and I did it clean, and I've had three weeks to enjoy it. I want you to understand how clean it sounded. I remember exactly how clean it sounded.
Mr. Morrow.

dialogueBeats.expression: low, and it costs him not to shout it
dialogueBeats.text: Was it you. Just — tell me straight, don't make me stand here and guess like a fucking idiot.
The house. Four hours north.
Yeah.
The yard.

dialogueBeats.expression: a beat — the first thing that lands on him
dialogueBeats.text: I know. I was closer than I wanted to be.
He didn't know it was coming. If that's — I know that's not nothing to some people. He was still running. He never turned round.
He didn't know it was coming. If that's — I know that's not nothing to some people. He was home. The door was shut. He never did hear it.

action.text: Something old and warped. It plays a recording, Desh. That's all it is.

scenes.title: Part 4b — The Blue Cue, Again
scenes.prose: Jack hasn't reached the door. The room talks him through it one last time — then lets him go.

dialogueBeats.text: Why are you telling me that.
'Cause you're gonna build a worse one in your head every night for the rest of your life, and I'd rather you had the true one to put against it.
That's the part nobody warns you about. I came in here ready for them to be monsters. They weren't. They were two men at a bar who did a job, remembered a detail, and thought I might want it.
You want to do something about it, now's the time. Nobody in here'd stop you and I wouldn't blame you.
Would you fight back?
Yeah. But I'd feel bad about it.
And there it was. The whole town in one sentence. Everybody's willing, nobody's cruel, and the arithmetic gets done anyway.

dialogueBeats.expression: calling after him, and he means it — a beat after 'wouldn't say'
dialogueBeats.text: Hey — Morrow. For what it's worth. He didn't give her up. They asked him where she was and he wouldn't say. Six hundred bucks got us the house. Nothing got us her.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — spare, breaking — a beat after 'wouldn't say her name'
dialogueBeats.text: Two hundred and eleven thousand dollars in a bag and eleven hours where she could have called him, and at the end of it he still wouldn't say her name. I've thought about which one of us that makes the fool. I keep getting the same answer and I keep not liking it.

dialogueBeats.expression: last line, to Desh, casual, back to it

scenes.title: Part 5 — The Trade
scenes.prose: An office above the shuttered feed store — the least impressive room in Blackwood, which is the point. A space heater ticking. Rain on a single window. Friday. Ten past nine in the morning.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — spare — a beat after 'in the morning'
dialogueBeats.text: Solomon Reyes doesn't have a compound. He's got a room over the feed store with a space heater and a filing cabinet. I used to think that was humility. It isn't. It's confidence. You don't need a fortress in a town that can't leave.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat. A chair. Two men sitting. And — audible for the first time — the shift of two more bodies against a wall behind Jack.
dialogueBeats.text: Moe and Desh were by the door. Not sitting. That's the difference between a conversation and a room somebody's controlling the exits on.
Mr. Morrow. I heard you were standing there. I'm sorry about that — the standing there part. I want you to know it wasn't an instruction.
Wasn't it.
It was a permission. There's a difference. It matters to me even if it doesn't matter to you.
I'm here about the Voss debt.
Of course you are. It's Friday.
It's Friday. Say what you're going to say, Solomon, I don't have the patience today.

dialogueBeats.expression: mild, not gloating — a beat after 'a decision'
dialogueBeats.text: I did wonder whether you'd come today or Thursday. Thursday would have been panic. Today's a decision. I prefer decisions.
The forty-eight hours. You never said they stopped.

I stopped counting it the moment there was a body — a clock's a way of making somebody hurry, and you'd stopped needing one. I didn't mention it because you'd have taken it as mercy, and it wasn't. It was housekeeping.
Put it on me.

dialogueBeats.expression: a long pause. The heater. Rain. Behind Jack — Moe shifting his weight. A jacket settling over something with weight in the pocket.

Only investigator in this county who doesn't work for you.

dialogueBeats.text: I told him. That was the job. Drive four hours and be the worst news a man's ever had.
He was making tea when I said it. He'd got two mugs out because I was there. I said Solomon's got your wife in a room above the feed store, and he put the second mug back in the cupboard.

dialogueBeats.expression: nothing. The engine. Rain. Held far too long.

dialogueBeats.text: Because a man who's agreed to give it back isn't a debtor any more. He's just somebody who knows things. Solomon didn't want him found. He wanted him decided. Once he'd decided, he was finished.
I did that. Not Moe, not Desh, not the man over the feed store. I drove four hours and gave a decent man a reason to say the one sentence that got him shot, and then I got back in the car.

Four hours back to a town where the only person who'll talk to me is the man holding her.

dialogueBeats.text: He let me up. Course he did. He'd been waiting for me to arrive so the room could do the rest.

dialogueBeats.expression: the radiator. Rain on the window.

No.
No. It wouldn't.

All of it. He told me everything before —
Before.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat, and now the confession comes — not extracted, offered
dialogueBeats.text: Fourteen months. Two hundred and eleven thousand. I picked the date, I built the folder, I picked you. My father borrowed four thousand pounds for a furnace in 2011 and it was eleven when he died and Solomon shook my hand at the funeral.
Vera—

dialogueBeats.text: And there were eleven hours where I knew they had the address and I didn't ring him. I sat in my kitchen doing arithmetic.
So don't stand there looking like the guilty one. There's a queue.

That's the confession. Not in a wet lot behind a mill with the rain coming down — in an armchair, in a warm room, with a cold cup of tea, because she'd had nineteen hours to get it into order and nothing else to do.
What does he want.
He hasn't said. He's waiting for me to offer.
Course he is.

scenes.title: Act Three, Part 3 — Nothing In My Pockets
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 3 — Nothing In My Pockets
scenes.prose: Jack's office. No lamp on. Rain on the window. The folder from Act One still on the desk.

dialogueBeats.text: I sat in my own office in the dark for two hours working out what I had. Sixteen years of files. Every cop I still know. Every person in this town who talks to me because I don't talk to him.
Worth something to a man buying a reputation. Worth nothing at all to a man who's already holding the thing you want, because he doesn't have to buy it — he can just wait.
That's the difference nobody tells you about. A debt you can pay. A hostage you can only beg for.

dialogueBeats.expression: a phone picked up. Dialled. Ringing.

dialogueBeats.text: I rang Rosa at three in the morning and hung up before it connected. Twice.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — flat — a beat after 'out of the room'
dialogueBeats.text: Not because she'd have refused. Because she'd have come. She'd have come and she'd have brought a badge into a building where a woman's sitting in an armchair being politely not-detained, and there is no version of that where Vera gets out of the room.

dialogueBeats.expression: a long hold. Rain on the window.

dialogueBeats.text: Sixteen years I kept one thing back and the first time it'd actually be useful, using it would kill her. That's not a moral position. That's just how the arithmetic came out.
So I went up there with nothing in my pockets and offered him everything anyway.

choices.text: Up the stairs. Nothing in his pockets.

scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 4 — The Trade
scenes.prose: The feed store office. Ten past nine. Same room, same heater. Rain on one window. Moe and Desh against the wall, unannounced.

Mr. Morrow. She's had breakfast. I'd like that noted.
Noted.
And David?
I know. I'm asking whether you'd like to say it, because I find people generally do.
He said he'd bring it back. Straight away. No arguing.
Did he. That's a better man than I had him down for.
Then why.

dialogueBeats.expression: without cruelty, which is the horror — a beat after 'an asset'
dialogueBeats.text: Because I'd have had the money and a man walking round who'd agreed to give it back. One of those is an asset.
Let her go.
She's not being kept.
She's in a room above a feed store with two of your men on the stairs.
She's welcome to leave whenever she likes. She simply understands what leaving means, which is not the same as being prevented.

dialogueBeats.expression: Moe shifting his weight. A jacket settling over something with weight in the pocket.

dialogueBeats.text: Then take the debt off her and put it on me.
With what.

dialogueBeats.expression: the terms — a beat after 'Take that'
dialogueBeats.text: Sixteen years of files. Every contact I've got. The licence in a drawer. I'm the only investigator in this county who doesn't work for you. Take that.

dialogueBeats.expression: a long pause. Rain. The heater.
quietly, and this is the route's central line
dialogueBeats.text: Mr. Morrow. Two days ago that would have been the most interesting offer anyone's made me in a decade.

dialogueBeats.expression: unhurried — a beat after 'how little it takes'
dialogueBeats.text: But you gave me her name in a pool hall, for nothing, to see whether a man would blink. I already know what you'll hand over and how little it takes. There's nothing left to buy.

dialogueBeats.expression: the heater ticking. A very long hold.
V.O. — spare — a beat after 'the price'
dialogueBeats.text: Sixteen years. He didn't want it. Not because it wasn't worth anything — because I'd already shown him the price.

dialogueBeats.expression: after a moment, standing, going to the window
dialogueBeats.text: Here's what will happen, and you may as well hear it sitting down.
The debt stays where it is. She'll pay on it, the way her father did, the way people here do. Nobody will hurt her. Nobody will need to.
That's not —

dialogueBeats.expression: not raising his voice at all — a beat after 'in a bar'
dialogueBeats.text: And you'll stay too. Not because I'm keeping you — because you won't leave her, and she can't leave. I've not had to arrange a single part of this, Mr. Morrow. You did it yourself in a bar.
You may collect her. She's not been charged with anything and neither have you. That's the whole of it. There's no more to the arrangement than that.
He didn't know it was coming. If that's — I know that's not nothing to some people. He was home. The door was shut. He never did hear it.

dialogueBeats.expression: calling after him, and he means it — a beat after 'got us the house'
dialogueBeats.text: Hey — Morrow. For what it's worth. Six hundred bucks got us the house. Nothing got us her.

scenes.title: Act Three, Part 5 — Nobody's Witness
scenes.partBreak: Act Three, Part 5 — Nobody's Witness
scenes.prose: The Blackwood Diner. Friday. Eleven forty-seven. The same booth. Vera opposite him, coat on, no bag — she was never packing, she was upstairs.

dialogueBeats.text: I collected her from a room above a feed store and we walked to a diner because neither of us could think where else people go.
He let us both out.
He didn't have to let us out. That's the point he was making.
I know. I got it.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after 'understood that correctly'
dialogueBeats.text: So I owe two hundred and twenty-two thousand pounds to a man who employs half this town, and I'll be paying on it when I'm sixty, and you've got nothing left to sell because he wouldn't take it. Have I understood that correctly.
Yeah.
Right.

scenes.title: Part 5 — What He Told Her
scenes.prose: The song enters — stripped, a fragment, low. Same melody as the Interlude. It does not swell.

dialogueBeats.text: There's a thing you should have.
Go on.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat, careful — a beat after 'Not for a second'
dialogueBeats.text: When I told him they had you, he had a mug in his hand and he put it back in the cupboard and said "right, I'll bring it back." Didn't think about it. Not for a second.
Don't.
Six hundred quid got them the house. Nothing got them you. They asked him and he wouldn't say.

dialogueBeats.expression: her breaking — short, ugly, stopped fast.

dialogueBeats.text: Eleven hours. I had eleven hours and I sat there doing sums—
I know.
—and he put a mug in a cupboard.

dialogueBeats.expression: rain. The song. A long silence.
after a long time, steadier, and this is why she stays
dialogueBeats.text: There's no bus.
There's a bus at six.

dialogueBeats.expression: flat — a beat after 'don't know anybody'
dialogueBeats.text: There's no bus, Jack. I owe him two hundred and twenty-two thousand pounds. The bus goes to a place where I owe him two hundred and twenty-two thousand pounds and don't know anybody.

dialogueBeats.expression: very quiet — a beat after 'twice in one week'
dialogueBeats.text: I'd worked out I was going to leave you. On the walk down here. It was quite a good plan. And then you told me that, and now I know exactly what it costs when somebody puts a mug in a cupboard for me, and I can't do it twice in one week.
Stay.

dialogueBeats.expression: and she means all of it
dialogueBeats.text: I want to. That's how I know it's a bad idea.

dialogueBeats.expression: a long hold. Rain. The fan. Neither of them moving.

dialogueBeats.text: I'm not going to, though.
I know.

dialogueBeats.expression: the fan. Rain. The song underneath, not resolving.

dialogueBeats.text: Nobody drove off. Nobody said anything that'd look good written down. Two people sat in a booth owing the same man the same money, and started the long part.

scenes.title: Part 5 — The Thing He Kept
scenes.prose: The fan. The rain. Jack not speaking. The song, thin, underneath.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — spare — a beat after 'I kept it'
dialogueBeats.text: I had one thing left that was mine to give. A mug going back in a cupboard. And I looked at what it'd do to her and I decided she'd had enough for one week, and I kept it.
You've gone quiet.
Long day.

dialogueBeats.expression: standing, coat still on — a beat after 'then I don't know'
dialogueBeats.text: Right. Well. I'm two doors down till the end of the month and then I don't know.
Okay.

dialogueBeats.expression: at the edge of the booth, and there's nothing in it

dialogueBeats.expression: the bell. The door. Rain swelling — then muffled.
the fan. The rain. Jack alone. The song, thin.

Sixteen years of not handing things over. Turns out I only ever got it wrong in the two directions available.

scenes.title: Part 6 — She Stays

endingData.headline: SHE STAYS
endingData.recap: A woman said 'I'm not going to, though,' and a sentence took three days to finish. In this town, that's about as close to a happy ending as anybody's ever come.

scenes.prose: The booth. Two people owing the same man the same money, and the long part.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — spare — a beat after 'any less dead'
dialogueBeats.text: People think the hard part is losing them. The hard part is the part after. Where you got what you wanted, and it's sitting across the table looking at you, and neither of you can think of the thing to say that makes a man in a yard four hours north any less dead.

dialogueBeats.expression: V.O. — almost nothing — rain, the fan, the song thinning; a beat after 'tipped a motel clerk'
dialogueBeats.text: He tipped a motel clerk. Nine days out, two hundred grand in a bag, sleeping in his shoes — and he tipped a motel clerk. I still can't put it down. Neither can she. That's most of what we've got in common now, and it's more than some people have.

dialogueBeats.expression: quiet, out of nowhere, the first thing either of them has said in a long time
dialogueBeats.text: Doors.

dialogueBeats.expression: not looking up — rain, the fan
dialogueBeats.text: He used to say a shut door is just a wall that's lying about it.
I remembered it. Three days. I've been trying to remember it for three days.

dialogueBeats.expression: silence. Neither of them says anything else.

dialogueBeats.text: She got it back. That's the one thing that came back. Eleven fifty-one on a Friday, a woman sat back down in a booth, and a sentence took three days to finish, and in this town that's about as close to a happy ending as anybody's ever come.

dialogueBeats.expression: the song — holding — then not resolving. It stops, the way the vocal does. Rain. The fan. Silence.

scenes.prose: Rain. The sodium light. Ten feet of gravel between them, neither of them crossing it.

And no, I didn't find out about the yard from you. I knew before. I've known since the address was sold.
She knew before the yard. I want that on the record. I don't know what it makes her. I know what it makes the eleven hours.

dialogueBeats.text: The form. What are you giving up.
The last thing in this town I still thought was worth staying for. Sign it and Monday I'm somebody else's problem — actual budget, backup that shows up, a case that isn't this one.

And I want you to understand the part you can't see: I've done the arithmetic too. If I help you and it goes bad, that form never gets signed. Nobody moves a detective who let a killing walk to protect a friend.
I know.

No.

You found out at thirty-four. I've thought about you, on and off, for ten years. Not as a problem. As a curiosity.
And now you've walked up my stairs to sell it to me for a woman whose father I said no to.
Yes.

dialogueBeats.text: Now I'm older, and there's a man dead in a house four hours north because I gave permission for it, and I find I don't like the arithmetic as much as I used to. Take the deal off the table before I remember I'm a businessman.

dialogueBeats.text: I put sixteen years on a desk in a room over a feed store and I walked down the stairs. Eleven months at an empty desk, because I wouldn't lose one file. Ten years of nothing after, because I wouldn't. That was the whole thing I was.
